questions.title: Confusion over the dual standards of review for JMOL and jury findings in Federal Circuit appeals
questions.question_body: I'm reading the discussion section where the court says they review the denial of JMOL under Fifth Circuit law (de novo, reversing only if evidence points 'strongly and overwhelmingly' to one party) but then says they review the jury's finding of infringement for 'substantial evidence.' I'm confused—isn't the JMOL motion essentially asking the court to review the jury's finding? Why are there two different standards of review being applied to the same outcome (the infringement verdict)?

questions.title: How does 'sampling' work in the context of the '134 patent's non-infringement ruling?
questions.question_body: In the '134 patent analysis, the court reverses because the 'modeled PIM path' is generated *after* the RF ADC sampling occurs. The court says signals cannot be sampled before they are generated. For a non-lawyer/student, I'm struggling to understand why this is a fatal blow to the infringement claim. If the system eventually processes these signals, why does the specific sequence of sampling vs. generation matter so much for the 'interference generating signals' limitation?

questions.title: What is the distinction between 'unique' signals and 'separately identifiable' signals in claim construction?
questions.question_body: Regarding the '775 patent, the court held that 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' does not require the signals to be 'unique,' only 'separately identifiable.' The court then suggests that using two unique signals plus a copy of one of them satisfies this. I don't understand the legal or technical distinction here. If S3 is just a copy of S1, isn't that still just two unique signals? How can a copy be 'separately identifiable' without being 'unique'?

questions.title: Why wasn't the amendment from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals' considered a clear disavowal of scope?
questions.question_body: In the '775 patent section, Finesse amended their claims during prosecution to change 'two or three signals' to 'three signals' to overcome a prior art rejection (Filipovic). Usually, when a patentee narrows a claim to get it allowed, they are seen as surrendering the surrendered scope. Why did the court find that this amendment did *not* rise to the level of a 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal of products using only two unique input signals?

questions.title: Does a patent claim for 'seven multiplications' require an exact 1:1 mapping even if the device performs more than seven?
questions.question_body: At oral argument, Finesse claimed the accused radios actually perform ten multiplications, which is more than the seven required by the '775 patent. However, the court still found non-infringement because Finesse couldn't map a specific subset of those ten to the seven claimed multiplications. If a device does *more* than what the patent requires, why is the failure to provide a precise mapping of the subset sufficient to reverse the infringement verdict?

questions.title: What is the procedural effect of 'vacating' the damages award versus 'reversing' it?
questions.question_body: The court reverses the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and then 'vacates' the damages award. I'm confused by the terminology. Since the court found there was no infringement, the damages logically cannot exist, but why use the term 'vacate' for the damages while using 'reverse' for the JMOL ruling? Does this have different legal implications for the finality of the judgment?
